Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

BitChat is not a covert network. It is a Bluetooth mesh: nearby phones form a local cluster, and a message hops through other phones about seven hops, a few hundred metres in good conditions. No account. No phone number. No central server. Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted. Built for a crowd, a protest, a blackout, a disaster zone. Not city-wide messaging.
The public record of misuse is thin. The documented Indian spike is July 2026, around the Jantar Mantar protests. India briefly accounted for most of the app’s global downloads. The official line was “substantial risk of misuse.” No reported case of a serious offence is in the open record.
Police cannot do with this what they do with WhatsApp or a telecom operator. That fear can exist. It is not evidence the app has been used for a serious crime in India.
Section 69A lets the Centre order an intermediary to block public access to information on grounds such as security or public order. Apple’s notice says MeitY used it because the app “includes content that is illegal in India.” It does not name that content. The order has not been published.
The Court upheld 69A in Shreya Singhal only with safeguards: written reasons, a committee, a hearing, and a path to court. A secret whole-app removal is a different design.
Blocking the app, in secret, because it still works when the network is cut, is not the same as blocking a specific unlawful message. 🔪📵⚖️

Wuguan Master is the Arena's house strategy for crypto. Three trend signals, Supertrend, a weighted moving average cross and Ichimoku, vote on every closed candle, and a filter tied to Bitcoin's 200-week moving average decides when the strategy may trade at all.
Running a trend strategy on monthly candles is tempting: fewer trades, less noise, less time at the screen. For this strategy, that choice decides the result.

—
𝗢𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘀

On Bitcoin daily candles from January 2018 to September 2026, five saved runs averaged 36.0 percent a year. Holding Bitcoin over the same windows averaged 27.8 percent. The worst drop averaged 48 percent, with about 82 trades per run.
Five runs is exactly the platform's minimum for a reported figure, so this is a record of five, not a verdict. 𝗢𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗷𝗼𝗯.

—
𝗢𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘀

The same rules on monthly candles ran on 23 coins, one run each. They averaged minus 22.5 percent a year. Holding the same coins over the same windows averaged minus 1.6 percent.
22 of the 23 coins ended with a negative annual return. The one exception, TRX, made 28.1 percent a year, while holding TRX made 51.5 percent.
On Bitcoin, the monthly run made six trades between September 2021 and May 2026, and not one of them closed as a profitable round trip. It lost 14.9 percent a year while holding gained 28.2 percent.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿.

—
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

The three signals vote once per closed candle. On daily candles that is 365 votes a year, on monthly candles it is twelve.
A trend strategy wants to enter early in a move and leave when the move breaks. With one vote a month, a move can run for a month before the strategy confirms it, and fall for a month before the strategy leaves.
𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

"Monthly candles filter out noise. Shouldn't that help a trend strategy?"
Here it did the opposite. Filtering the noise also filtered the entries and exits, down to 3.8 trades per coin on average, and 22 of 23 coins finished in the red.

—
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼

Tested: Wuguan Master on monthly candles you can skip, which spares you a strategy that enters late and exits later.
Before you run any strategy, check which interval it was built and tested on, and treat every other interval as a new strategy that needs its own test.
The open question is the weekly candle. There, 50 runs averaged minus 0.6 percent a year against minus 24.7 percent for holding, which is better than holding, but on coins that mostly fell.

Study the Past — Improve your Future 🥋

text:
The new Indian IT Rules 2026 (Amendment) mandate labeling for AI-generated content (SGI: synthetic audio/visuals appearing real). Key points:

- Users declare AI use; platforms verify & add prominent labels + metadata for traceability.
- No unlabeled AI content allowed.
- Takedowns: 2-3 hours for deepfakes/objectionable material (down from 24-36h).
- Effective Feb 20, 2026.
- Non-compliance risks penalties under IT Act, loss of safe harbor for platforms.

Sources: Times of India, The Hindu, TechCrunch.

To,
The Grievance Officer / Legal Department
Meta Platforms / Facebook – India

Dear Sir/Madam,
https://t.co/ysy622TtcN

I, Hansraj Meena, Advocate practicing before the High Court and Supreme Court of India, hereby lodge this formal legal grievance regarding the repeated restriction of my Facebook content in India.

On 06 October 2026, Facebook displayed the following notice in relation to my post:

“Your photo is unavailable in India.”

The notice further states that the content has been restricted through an automated system pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.

I strongly object to such unexplained and opaque restriction of my content.

I hereby call upon Meta to disclose, in writing:

1. The exact statutory provision and section of law under which my post has been restricted.

2. Whether the restriction has been imposed pursuant to Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, or under any other statutory provision.

3. If Meta has received any Government direction, judicial order, notice or request concerning this content, provide the date, reference/order number, issuing authority and legal provision relied upon, subject to any legally permissible confidentiality.

4. If there is no Government or judicial order, clearly state whether the restriction was imposed solely under Meta’s internal policies.

5. Identify the exact Meta Community Standard or policy provision allegedly violated by my post.

6. Explain why the content has specifically been restricted in India.

7. Confirm whether the decision was made exclusively by an automated system and provide the applicable human-review and appeal mechanism.

8. Provide a proper, reasoned and legally intelligible decision enabling me to effectively challenge the restriction.

I specifically demand an immediate human review of the impugned restriction by an authorised Meta grievance/legal officer.

A generic statement referring to “legal requirements under Indian law” cannot, by itself, provide sufficient clarity regarding the precise legal basis of a restriction affecting access to published content.

I am fully conscious of the regulatory obligations applicable to intermediaries in India. However, lawful regulation cannot be used as a substitute for transparency and an effective grievance mechanism.

If Meta fails to provide the specific legal basis for the restriction, fails to conduct an effective review, or continues to restrict my content without lawful justification, I reserve my right to avail myself of all remedies available to me in law, including appropriate proceedings before the competent High Court and other appropriate forums.

I further request that all relevant records concerning this restriction, including the decision-making record, applicable policy, review history and communications relating to the restriction, be preserved to the extent legally permissible.

Treat this communication as a FORMAL LEGAL GRIEVANCE.

I expect a reasoned written response within the applicable grievance-redressal period.

Yours faithfully,

HANSRAJ MEENA
Advocate – High Court & Supreme Court of India

Nature of Grievance: Unexplained territorial restriction / automated content restriction / demand for legal basis and human review

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
An internet shutdown may look like a few kilometres marked on a government order. But its cost can look very different depending on who is standing inside that line.

This week on Decode This Week, we look at the unequal price of going offline.

Bitchat has been removed from India’s App Store after a government request.

The app has no servers or hosted content. It relays encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth.

If it has no content of its own, what exactly is being blocked?

📊 𝐋𝐄𝐆𝐀𝐋 𝐄𝐗𝐏𝐎𝐒𝐄: 𝐀 𝐁𝐋𝐀𝐍𝐊𝐄𝐓 𝐁𝐀𝐍 𝐃𝐈𝐒𝐆𝐔𝐈𝐒𝐄𝐃 𝐀𝐒 𝐀 𝐏𝐔𝐁𝐋𝐈𝐂 𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐄𝐑.
Delhi Police invoked Section 163 BNSS across the entire New Delhi district. Permission was denied. Section 163 prohibits assemblies of five or more, processions, dharnas, and even 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐚𝐧𝐬. This is not a public order measure. This is a blanket ban on dissent.

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐋𝐄𝐆𝐀𝐋 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐓𝐑𝐀𝐃𝐈𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍

Section 163 BNSS is meant for 𝐮𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 cases of nuisance or apprehended danger. The Supreme Court in 𝐌𝐚𝐝𝐡𝐮 𝐋𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐲𝐞 𝐯. 𝐒𝐮𝐛-𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 (1970) held that such orders must record 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 showing genuine, specific apprehension. Not boilerplate.

The Supreme Court in the 𝐑𝐚𝐦𝐥𝐢𝐥𝐚 𝐌𝐚𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 (2012) held that force under such an order must be 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞 to the actual threat. The State cannot assume a threat exists and act on that assumption.

The Delhi High Court in 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 stated: "𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐚 𝐛𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐧."

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐄𝐑'𝐒 𝐎𝐖𝐍 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐓𝐑𝐀𝐃𝐈𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍

The order was imposed across the 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐡𝐢 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭. The protest site itself was sealed. Barricades blocked entry from both Tolstoy Marg and Kerala Bhawan side. 11 Metro stations were closed. The internet was suspended. 4,000 police personnel deployed. Over 700 detained.

Permission was denied. Intimation was filed. The roads were blocked anyway.

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐐𝐔𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐄𝐑 𝐑𝐀𝐈𝐒𝐄𝐒

If the threat was imminent and specific, why did the order cover an entire district for an indefinite period? If the threat was not imminent, why was Section 163 invoked at all? The answer is the 𝐌𝐊𝐒𝐒 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭. In 2018, the Supreme Court examined Delhi Police's practice of renewing Section 144 notifications across Central Delhi every 60 days and called it what it was: a 𝐯𝐢𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐧 dressed up as a temporary, case-specific order.

𝐖𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐄𝐑 𝐁𝐀𝐍𝐒

▪ Assembly of five or more persons
▪ Processions, demonstrations, picketing, dharnas
▪ 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬

The third clause is the tell. An order that prohibits speech is not a public order measure. It is a gag order.

𝐏𝐑𝐎𝐕𝐄 𝐌𝐄 𝐖𝐑𝐎𝐍𝐆

Show the material facts recorded in this order that demonstrate a genuine, specific apprehension of danger. Show the intelligence report. Show me the threat assessment. Show why an entire district required a prohibitory order for a protest against an Election Commissioner.

If the order is about public safety, produce the safety assessment.
If it is about suppressing dissent, the courts have a name for that too.

Source: Daily Pioneer; Deccan Chronicle; Zee News; The Wire; Times of India; PTI.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

(1) 

Mobile internet services have been suspended in and around Jantar Mantar, Delhi, ahead of a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

(2)

The suspension order has not been published by the Government, and there is no publicly available information on the date and time of commencement, duration, or the specific area covered by the suspension.

(3)

Telecom service providers such as Jio have sent automated SMS alerts to subscribers in the affected areas stating: “As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice.”

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

The app was pulled from both the App Store and Google Play in India after a demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Apple's reason: "it includes content that is illegal in India."

What content? It's a local mesh app that hops messages over Bluetooth between nearby phones. There's no data center full of messages for anyone to rifle through.

The timing says it all. The ban came right after authorities shut off mobile internet for 12 hours during a protest in Delhi. Bitchat was built for exactly that situation. No cell towers, no Wi-Fi, no accounts, no phone numbers, no central server to raid. Just phones talking to each other.

Here's the thing India's government doesn't seem to understand: bitchat is free and open source. They can pressure Apple and Google to stop distributing it. They can't make the code disappear.

Android users can grab the APK from GitHub and sideload it. The app even has a "Share BitChat" feature that sends itself to another phone over a local hotspot. No internet required. One person with the app can spread it to everyone around them.

We saw what this looks like in practice last year when Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica. Bitchat jumped to the second most downloaded app on the island. When banking and communications went down, people used bitcoin to move money and bitchat to talk to each other.

Download bitchat before you need it. App Store, Google Play, or the APK. You might not use it for a year. But when the towers go down or your government decides you shouldn't be able to talk to your neighbors, you'll be glad it's on your phone.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

text:
Towards Fast Disposal of Court Cases in India and Making Judiciary Accountable

With about five crore cases pending in courts and tribunals of this country, India perhaps may be on top in cases in courts and tribunals both in respect of  total number of cases and even according to court-cases proportionate to population thus making a much larger number of families and individuals always involved in tense-filled costly litigations paving way for judicial corruption at all levels with even Madras High Court confessing -None can deny there is corruption in judiciary, judges are not holy cows- with India ranking poorly at 86th place out of 143 countries in WJP Rule of Law Index. Corruption in Indian Judicial System is also a factor for India ranking poorly at 96th place out of total 180 countries in Corruption Perception Index while ranking at 118th place out of total 147 countries in World Happiness Report.

Fast disposal of cases in Indian courts and tribunals on lines of developed countries can to some extent can overcome the problem as highlighted here-above. Much of time in Indian courts is spent on long adjournments where petitioners go on seeking adjournment after adjournment after managing an ex-party stay-order on first day of hearing. Division Bench of Supreme Court comprising of Justices RV Ravindran and JM Panchal in January 2009 observed and rightly too of the bitter reality that at times those having taken ex-party stay-orders seeking frequent adjournments in most cases ultimately lose the cases. Adjournments may be given only in exceptional cases. Court-cases should be contested mainly on basis of written arguments rather than on basis of oral arguments so that no law-point may be missing from records while there are every chances that oral arguments may not be fully become part of court-verdicts. System will again avoid adjournment-culture where at many times adjournments are sought on basis of non-appearance of arguing lawyers due to various reasons. Such a system will make litigations less costly because of less need of costly senior-designated lawyers required for oral arguments. Rather system of having senior-designated lawyers should be abolished altogether.

Modern technology can further add to reduction of court-cases. Cheque-bouncing cases filed under section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act can be drastically reduced by inserting a QR-code on every cheque where decoding of QR code may reveal complete details of cheques bounced from the bank-account/s may be available.

Another reason for such large number of court-cases is Perjury where it has become a usual tradition to speak lie in Indian courts and to file false affidavits with extremely low conviction-rate making wrong-doers worriless with no fear of law leading to a high crime-rate. Rajasthan High Court had to once direct action against two Oath Commissioners having attested an affidavit while the applicant was out of the country. Such an illegal practice is quite common when usually Oath Commissioners and Notary Public fulfill formality of attesting documents without verifying the person or signature whose signatures are to be attested. Phenomenon of Oath-Commissioners and Notary Public where they usually charge fees much in excess than fixed by the government should be totally abolished. Instead power of attestation should be given to every registered lawyer. This will induce at least some accountability on lawyers too when they will be attesting for their clients. Power of attestation can also be given chartered-accountants, medical-practitioners, officers of government and public-sector-undertakings. Station-House-Officers (SHOs) of police-stations who presently do not have such powers, may be authorized and duty-bound to free-of-cost attest documents of those who do not have easy access to authorities mentioned above.

India is perhaps the only country where judges recommend to appoint judges in higher judiciary resulting in a constant tussle between legislature and judiciary. Collegium-system at Supreme Court for recommending appointments and transfers at Supreme Court and High Courts is also at times under criticism for some selected families observed as dominating Indian judiciary. It may also not be advisable to hand over appointment in higher judiciary solely in hands of political hands of legislature. A balanced approach can be achieved by instituting a high-powered National Judicial Commission having retired Supreme Court judges as member-nominees of President, Prime Minister, Leader of largest Opposition Party in Lok Sabha, Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Bar Council of India with Chief Vigilance Commissioner as ex-officio member of the Commission with Union Law Secretary as ex-officio member-secretary of such a Commission. CJI may head such a high-powered Commission. Recommendations of such a Commission should be final, and sent directly to President of India for a formal endorsement. Retirement-age of High Court judges should be raised to 65 years to be at par with that of Supreme Court judges to avoid any chances of lobbying for promotion as Supreme Court judges only because to be in system for three extra years. Reforms for future may be there to establish Indian Judicial Service (IJS) on lines of Indian Administrative Service (IAS) where those passing the tough competition may be appointed first at District Courts and ultimately to be elevated first to High Courts and then to Supreme Court.

To prevent chances of influencing locally appointed High Court judges either through their former bar-colleagues or local relations, all High Court judges should be compulsorily appointed outside from their home-states. To eliminate political bias in judiciary, it should be ensured that no person may be appointed as judge with an active political background. Even after retirement if any judge joins politics, he must lose all his post-retirement benefits. No judge should be given any post-retirement job anywhere after two years of retirement. It should be ensured that any person seated as CJI must get at least one year to be on post before he attains retirement-age of 65 years. Indian system is witness of contrast cases with Justice Kamal Narain Singh having been CJI for just 18 days (25.11.1991 to 12.12.1991) while Justice Yeshwant Vishnu Chandrachud having been CJI for more than seven years (22.02.1978 to 11.07.1985).

Suggested National Judicial Commission should also be empowered to probe all complaints against judges including Chief Justices of Supreme Court and High Courts, abolishing cumbersome and impractical system of removal of tainted judges through impeachment. It is noteworthy that in present system, there is no disciplinary authority for Chief Justice of India. Findings of the Commission and punishment suggested for such guilty-found judges should be endorsed for action with all post-retirement benefits of such tainted judges abolished. Even nothing could be done in the first-ever impeachment-case of Justice V Ramaswamy where the motion fell because of north-south divide of legislature. Tax-payers’ hard-earned money was wasted in paying a judge of a High Court for no work while on post and after retirement after the Supreme Court Collegium decided to recommend his impeachment. Judges are also human-beings picked up from the same society which has both honest and dishonest persons. Chairs of judges are not made from some divine material which can turn some undesirable one found entry as judge to turn fair.

Status of Chief Justice of India should be made at par with that of Union Cabinet Secretary, and of all other Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts at par with that Secretary in the Government in all respects of monetary and other benefits while on post and after retirement. However, for protocol purposes, Chief Justice of India and other Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, existing position may be maintained. No extra-ordinary privileges should be provided to retired judges which presently also include life-time domestic help for them and their spouses after deaths of retired judges. Since pensions to government-employees has been done away, same system should be there for those in judiciary (and even in legislature).

All judges from Supreme Court to trial-courts must compulsorily record reason for recusal from the case on the file. Moreover, any such recusal should be informed immediately so that a new bench may be there for hearing without requiring any postponement of the hearing. A judge of Delhi High Court once recused herself from hearing a case where she herself issued notice to former President Pranab Mukerji after admitting a writ filed by some individual urging some contents of the book authored by the former President to be deleted. At times judges of higher courts have written to sitting Chief Justice of India about pressure and influence especially also from politicians. Making it compulsory to give reasons for recusal will prevent pressure and influence on judges.

Long summer vacations in courts were designed by erstwhile British rulers to save British judges in India from severe hot weather of this country, and also to facilitate them to visit their homeland. Unfortunately system continues in free India even after about eight long decades of independence, that too with long pendency of court-cases. Long-pending recommendation of Law Commission for scrapping long court-vacations should be implemented. Courts should adopt normal government-calendars for holidays abolishing system of week-long vacations for religious festivals apart from long winter and summer vacations.

Whole system of continuing naming High Courts is confusing where some High Courts are still named after cities where these are situated. Indian cities Bombay, Madras, Allahabad have since been renamed as Mumbai, Chennai and Prayag respectively long time back. But High Courts located in these cities are still officially named after old names of these cities. System should be that names of High Courts may get auto-changed with change in names of cities. Best is to end the British legacy by naming all High Courts after names of states rather than on cities. Proposed legislation should incorporate feature that names of High Courts may be automatically changed with change in name of states without needing any separate legislation. 

#JudicialReforms #IndianJudiciary #SpeedyJustice #JudiciaryAccountability #JusticeWithoutDelay #CourtCasePendency #LegalReforms #IndianLegalSystem #JudicialTransparency #SupremeCourtOfIndia #DigitalCourts #AccessToJustice #JusticeForAll #CourtReforms

The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES) is expanding cooperation with civil society and youth networks to curb online gambling and reduce access to illegal websites. The approach includes greater public participation, closer coordination with digital platforms and search engines, and wider use of technology to detect gambling-related content.

Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob met anti-gambling organizations on October 5 to discuss measures to protect the public, especially children and young people. MDES plans to expand channels for reporting information, tips, and experiences involving online gambling, with a working group analyzing the information and coordinating with digital platforms. Relevant cases may also be forwarded to the Royal Thai Police for legal action.

The ministry will work with search engines to make gambling-related websites and information more difficult to access through online searches. Cooperation with the Education and Interior ministries and security agencies will also focus on raising awareness of gambling risks and safer social media use among children, students, and young people. MDES already uses artificial intelligence to identify gambling websites, alongside information received from law enforcement and the public.

During fiscal year 2026, court orders were obtained to block 835,207 gambling-related URLs, including 749,546 identified through MDES operations and 85,661 from Royal Thai Police information. Another 109,868 online items were blocked through coordination with digital platforms, bringing the reported total to 945,075 URLs and items.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Subject: FORMAL LEGAL GRIEVANCE – Unlawful and Unexplained Restriction of My Facebook Content in India
@facebook
@Meta
To,
The Grievance Officer / Legal Department
Meta Platforms / Facebook – India

Dear Sir/Madam,
https://t.co/ysy622TtcN

I, Hansraj Meena, Advocate practicing before the High Court and Supreme Court of India, hereby lodge this formal legal grievance regarding the repeated restriction of my Facebook content in India.

On 06 October 2026, Facebook displayed the following notice in relation to my post:

“Your photo is unavailable in India.”

The notice further states that the content has been restricted through an automated system pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.

I strongly object to such unexplained and opaque restriction of my content.

I hereby call upon Meta to disclose, in writing:

1. The exact statutory provision and section of law under which my post has been restricted.

2. Whether the restriction has been imposed pursuant to Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, or under any other statutory provision.

3. If Meta has received any Government direction, judicial order, notice or request concerning this content, provide the date, reference/order number, issuing authority and legal provision relied upon, subject to any legally permissible confidentiality.

4. If there is no Government or judicial order, clearly state whether the restriction was imposed solely under Meta’s internal policies.

5. Identify the exact Meta Community Standard or policy provision allegedly violated by my post.

6. Explain why the content has specifically been restricted in India.

7. Confirm whether the decision was made exclusively by an automated system and provide the applicable human-review and appeal mechanism.

8. Provide a proper, reasoned and legally intelligible decision enabling me to effectively challenge the restriction.

I specifically demand an immediate human review of the impugned restriction by an authorised Meta grievance/legal officer.

A generic statement referring to “legal requirements under Indian law” cannot, by itself, provide sufficient clarity regarding the precise legal basis of a restriction affecting access to published content.

I am fully conscious of the regulatory obligations applicable to intermediaries in India. However, lawful regulation cannot be used as a substitute for transparency and an effective grievance mechanism.

If Meta fails to provide the specific legal basis for the restriction, fails to conduct an effective review, or continues to restrict my content without lawful justification, I reserve my right to avail myself of all remedies available to me in law, including appropriate proceedings before the competent High Court and other appropriate forums.

I further request that all relevant records concerning this restriction, including the decision-making record, applicable policy, review history and communications relating to the restriction, be preserved to the extent legally permissible.

Treat this communication as a FORMAL LEGAL GRIEVANCE.

I expect a reasoned written response within the applicable grievance-redressal period.

Yours faithfully,

HANSRAJ MEENA
Advocate – High Court & Supreme Court of India
Facebook Page: Hans Chanda Official
Date: 07 October 2026
