Delhi Police's 'Selective Ethics': When Khaki Tramples the Law Underfoot, Dictating a 'Lakshman Rekha' to the Press is Administrative Audacity!

Author: Mithilesh Singh

In a democratic framework, the press stands as the critical fourth pillar, tasked with checking the absolute power of the ruling regime and the law enforcement machinery. However, the recent advisory issued by the Delhi Police outlining restrictive guidelines for journalists covering public protests has triggered a fierce constitutional and legal storm. Independent journalists, legal experts, and civil society are confronting the state with a direct question: does a police force heavily entangled in severe allegations of shredding human rights, the Rule of Law, and women’s safety possess even a shred of moral or constitutional authority to lecture the media on professional ethics?

Blatant Jurisdictional Breach and Administrative Overreach
According to established legal frameworks and the explicit statutes of the Press Council of India (PCI), the authority to regulate press freedom, dictate editorial methodologies, or enforce journalistic ethics rests solely with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting or the highest echelons of the judiciary. 

The Delhi Police department lacks the legal jurisdiction and constitutional standing to determine how independent journalism should operate on the ground.
Issuing such directives constitutes a flagrant breach of their administrative boundaries. Critics argue that ambiguous terms like "maintaining a safe distance" and "not obstructing police operations" are intentionally engineered. They serve as a legal shield to hide raw police brutality, unprovoked lathi charges, and illicit operational maneuvers from the lenses of the media, effectively strangling transparent and impartial reporting at the scene.
Guerrilla Tactics: Uniforms Devoid of Nameplates and Badges
Per mandatory directions issued by the Supreme Court—most notably in the landmark D.K. Basu vs. State of West Bengal case—every single law enforcement officer on duty must visibly display a clear nameplate and an identifiable badge number. Yet, during recent capital protests, this foundational legal requirement was casually crushed under police boots.

while lowest-tier personnel are deployed with identifying gear, high-ranking officers orchestrating operations deliberately strip nameplates and badges from their uniforms. When confronted, they shield themselves behind the repetitive, shameless excuse that their badges "fell off in the chaos." Civil rights organizations rightly label this a calculated strategy. By obscuring their identities, these officers insulate themselves from future legal accountability, giving them a free hand to inflict atrocities on journalists and peaceful protestors with absolute impunity.

The Grim Truth Behind Viral Content
The supreme irony of this entire crisis is spotlighted by damning video evidence and viral social media reels that exposed the true face of the force. In widely circulated footage, an officer—identified as ACP Bhagat—was caught on camera aggressively violating the modesty of a female protestor and journalist, physically harassing her to stifle independent coverage.

Instead of immediate suspension, arrest, and prosecution under the law, reports suggest the department chose to reward such misconduct with an administrative promotion. A furious public demands to know: how can a department that shelters components guilty of molesting citizens and concealing identities dare to preach ethics to the press? When those sworn to uphold the constitution choose to trample it day and night, their attempts to discipline the fourth pillar represent the absolute zenith of institutional hypocrisy.

In a constitutional democracy, no uniform, rank, or state agency can place itself above the supreme law of the land.

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

As President of the Movie Artistes Association, I want to make it clear that MAA is compiling information on accounts and networks repeatedly involved in targeted abuse and malicious campaigns, including accounts misusing actors’ photographs and identities to mislead people.

This is NOT about stopping criticism.

It is about accountability.

The present deepfake incident makes the larger conversation urgent. And unfortunately, this will not be the last deepfake. Technology is moving too quickly for us to believe deleting one video or filing one complaint solves the problem.

I request the Telugu Film Chamber, Producers Council, MAA and all stakeholders to sit together and create a permanent industry-wide mechanism to address AI deepfakes, impersonation, coordinated malicious campaigns and deliberate online sabotage.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

A man told the Delhi High Court that a 12-minute recording of him was an AI voice clone.

That's the quiet cost of deepfakes: any real recording can now be denied. Proof has to be set at the moment of recording.

A man was arrested in Rajasthan after investigators say he used AI-generated videos of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and actor Vijay to lure people into a financial scam.

The fake videos showed Vijay speaking Hindi and were distributed through Facebook and other social platforms. Targets were then moved into WhatsApp conversations connected to the alleged fraud.

Trust

Last week the US Justice Department charged two men over an alleged scheme to sell counterfeit Ozempic from China to US distributors.

US law requires a unique serial number on every package of a prescription drug. The counterfeit cartons carried false serial numbers, and one of them, 430834149057, is on every unit in the shipments it lists: about 47 units in September 2023, 924 in November, and 1,008 ten days later.

This is a very well established pattern for counterfeiters: put something plausible on the packaging, no-one will have the time to actually check it.

This time though.. someone did! In fact on 19 November 2023 an alleged co-conspirator warned that every unit had the same serial number, and that a trading partner who noticed would have to quarantine it and report it to the FDA. 

In December the FDA published that exact serial number in a public warning. A contact at one of the buyers asked whether the warning would affect a pending order for 60,000 more units. and of course one of the two men charged, replied: "Not at all."

A public warning only covers the serial number the FDA has already found, and the next batch can carry a different one. The cloned serial only flares red when someone compares serial numbers across cartons and deliveries. So the practical question is: would the receiving process of warehouses/distributors flag the anomaly? Apparently very few do because it takes a lot of time.

Btw, this is exactly one of the use cases for EUIPO Authentic View standard and one of the reasons why I started Eonpass: you have to dig into the supply chain to understand what's happening, looking at labels is one of the many steps in an investigation.

Three provisions of the DPDP framework commence on 13 November 2026, which is 39 days from today. Section 6(9) of the Act requires every Consent Manager to be registered with the Data Protection Board, and Rule 4 of the DPDP Rules sets the conditions for that registration. A Consent Manager is a company through which a person can give, manage and withdraw consent across businesses.

Section 27(1)(d) of the Act commences on the same day and lets the Board inquire into a breach of a Consent Manager's registration conditions. The Board has no chairperson and no members, and MeitY has not published an application form, a portal or a fee for registration.

The question is not who voted for whom.

The fundamental question is:

WHY WERE VOTERS’ NAMES REMOVED FROM THE ELECTORAL ROLLS?

In this interview, Brinda Karat raises a series of direct questions about the removal of voters' names, the role of the Election Commission and the consequences of the present SIR exercise.

Her central argument is simple:

THE RIGHT TO VOTE BELONGS TO EVERY ELIGIBLE INDIAN CITIZEN.

If a citizen was already on the electoral roll, why should that citizen suddenly have to fight to establish their right to remain there?

And if large numbers of names have disappeared from the rolls, the first responsibility of the electoral system should be to provide transparent reasons, individual verification and an effective opportunity for restoration.

The interview also raises questions about the 2023 change in electoral law and argues that the change should be reconsidered.

Most importantly, it demands that the SIR process itself be stopped and subjected to public scrutiny.

These are not questions that should be answered through political rhetoric.

They require documents, electoral-roll data, deletion reasons, BLO records, verification trails and transparent accountability.

THREE QUESTIONS FOR THE ELECTION COMMISSION

1️⃣ WHY WAS EACH VOTER'S NAME REMOVED?

Give the affected voter a clear, verifiable reason.

2️⃣ WHAT CHANGED IN THE LAW IN 2023 — AND WHY?

The public deserves to understand the legal basis and consequences of that change.

3️⃣ WHAT SAFEGUARDS EXIST AGAINST THE WRONGFUL EXCLUSION OF ELIGIBLE VOTERS DURING SIR?

A voter should not have to discover their disenfranchisement only when they attempt to vote.

The integrity of an electoral roll is measured not merely by how efficiently names are removed.

It is measured by whether every eligible citizen can remain on the roll and exercise the franchise without arbitrary or unexplained exclusion.

VERIFY EVERY DELETION.
PROTECT EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTER.
PUBLISH THE REASONS.
PROVIDE AN EFFECTIVE REMEDY.

Democracy cannot be reduced to the question of who won an election.

Before that comes the more fundamental question:

WHO WAS ALLOWED TO REMAIN ON THE ELECTORAL ROLL?

text:
Global Access Map: Where Starlink is Blocked or Awaiting Approval
While SpaceX’s Starlink now operates in over 100 countries, significant global coverage gaps remain due to geopolitical sanctions, state security policies, and pending spectrum licenses.
1. Restricted & State-Banned Nations
(Blocked due to state monopolies, security restrictions, or international sanctions)
 * China: Banned to protect domestic space and satellite constellations (Guowang / Qianfan).
 * Russia: Banned due to national security concerns and military restrictions.
 * Iran: Blocked locally under strict state internet control and US sanctions.
 * North Korea: Total state-enforced telecommunications blackout.
 * Syria: Under comprehensive international sanctions and state regulatory blocks.
 * Cuba: Restricted under US embargo provisions and state telecommunications law.
 * Belarus: Blocked under regional security arrangements and active sanctions.
 * Afghanistan: Unapproved under current administrative and telecommunications rules.
 * Myanmar: Banned by the military regime, with strict prohibitions on satellite hardware.
 * Venezuela: Lacks operational authorization and regulatory agreements.
2. Pending Regulatory & Spectrum Approvals
(Applications submitted or trials underway, awaiting final commercial clearance)
 * India: Awaiting finalized administrative spectrum allocations, pricing, and national security clearances.
 * South Africa: Held up by the mandatory 30% local equity ownership rule for telecom operators.
 * Pakistan: Pending technical and security evaluation by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA).
 * Vietnam: Subject to mandatory local data storage and joint-venture corporate requirements.
 * Thailand: Under review by the NBTC regarding foreign satellite licensing guidelines.
 * Turkey: Pending national spectrum assignment and BTK regulatory approval.
 * Saudi Arabia: Ongoing discussions covering CITC licensing and localized infrastructure.
 * UAE: Commercial satellite broadband applications currently under review by TDRA.
 * Bangladesh: Technical trials completed; awaiting final spectrum license terms.
 * Egypt: Subject to military and national telecom regulatory agency approvals.
3. Regulatory Crackdowns on Grey-Market Imports
In several markets without direct licenses (notably Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Sudan, and Namibia), local telecom authorities have penalized the illicit importation of roaming terminals, prompting SpaceX to enforce geofencing until commercial licenses are granted.

text:
♦️Indian security agencies have paused final clearances for Starlink's commercial rollout, placing its foreign direct investment (FDI) proposal on hold over national security and ownership cross-holding concerns.

 🔶While Elon Musk’s satellite internet venture previously secured preliminary nods like the ⁠GMPCS license and ⁠IN-SPACe authorization, Indian authorities have heightened scrutiny following recent geopolitical conflicts where independent satellite terminals bypassed local restrictions.

🛑Key Regulatory Bottlenecks

🔶FDI and Cross-Holding Structures

💠The Issue: 
▶️The Indian government permits up to 100% FDI in satellite services, but automatic approval tops out at 74%. ▶️Starlink's proposal requires explicit clearance due to complex ⁠cross-holding structures involving parent company SpaceX and foreign investors.

🔶Network Control and Interception

💠The Issue: 
▶️Authorities want legally binding guarantees that the network can be intercepted or shut down locally during an emergency. 
▶️Rogue usage of satellite terminals in restricted regions globally has made Indian intelligence cautious.

🔷Data Localization Mandates

💠The Issue: 
▶️India mandates that all domestic user traffic must land and remain within geographical boundaries. 
▶️Starlink must prove that no data will be copied or decrypted overseas.

🔶Spectrum Allocation Holdup

💠The Issue: 
▶️The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and TRAI are still finalising administrative pricing frameworks for satellite spectrum.
▶️ Without the final assigned spectrum, a commercial launch is legally blocked.

🔷What Comes Next

▶️Starlink executives are engaged in ongoing discussions with ⁠Ministry of Commerce and telecom officials to iron out the structural discrepancies.
▶️ However, the government has made it clear that national security will not be compromised for speed of market entry.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

text:
If the concern is violence, why does this notice also tell someone to stay away from the protest?

That’s the part of the police notice shared by Abhijeet Dipke that needs a clear answer.

First, a small correction: this particular notice was addressed to a CJP supporter. It isn’t proof that Dipke himself received it.

The notice is from Ballarpur police, dated 5 October, and refers to the planned 10 October protest in Delhi. In simple words, it asks why the person wants to take part and who is providing financial support. It also tells them to stay away, warns against violence and provocative speeches, and mentions possible police action.

Getting this notice doesn’t mean someone has already committed a crime. It also doesn’t mean arrest is automatic.

The police have given their side. Chandrapur SP Ayush Nopany told Indian Express these are routine preventive notices, and permission for the protest is a matter for Delhi police.

Okay, then a few basic questions:

If Delhi gives permission, can this person attend peacefully?

What specific information makes police think this person might commit an offence?

Which law supports telling them to stay away, and must they answer the funding questions?

The notice also refers to a local restriction order. Can that order be made public, with an explanation of how it applies to attending an event in Delhi?

Preventing violence is important. So is giving ordinary people a clear answer about what they can lawfully do.

This is one notice. We shouldn’t assume every other notice says the same thing. But the questions about this one deserve proper answers.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
India's platforms are legally required to notify users when their content gets taken down by government order — but compliance is spotty at best.
The rule exists under the Information Technology Act's intermediary framework. When a platform receives a government takedown notice, users are supposed to get an explanation: what was removed, why, and which authority issued it.
In practice, most platforms either ignore this entirely or send vague notices after the fact. No timeline is enforced. No standardized format exists. Users often discover their content is gone only when they try to access it.
Former MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) cyber-law officials have flagged this gap repeatedly. The logic was simple: transparency about state censorship creates a paper trail, deters overreach, and lets users contest removals.
But India's digital ecosystem treats the notification rule as optional. WhatsApp doesn't notify for group bans. Twitter (now X) batches notices weeks later. YouTube compliance varies by region. TikTok, before its ban, rarely proactively informed users.
The enforcement gap matters because:
• There is no penalty structure — platforms face no fines or license consequences for skipping notification.
• Users have no realistic way to challenge removals without knowing they happened or why.
• Government agencies know the lack of oversight means takedowns go undocumented.
• A parallel system of private censorship operates without the judicial review that formal bans would trigger.
The fix would require either stricter intermediary rules with real penalties, or a centralized notification registry — both politically difficult in India's current regulatory environment.
As government content moderation requests accelerate globally, India's notification gap is becoming a template for how to make state censorship functionally invisible.

#MeitY #India #PlatformRegulation

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
WHEN THOSE WHO DEMAND JUSTICE ARE BEATEN, DEMOCRACY ITSELF IS ON TRIAL

What happened outside Parliament Street Police Station must not be allowed to disappear into the news cycle.

According to the testimonies presented in this report, journalists and young protesters spent the night outside the police station demanding something fundamental — that their complaint be registered and investigated. Instead, they have alleged detention, physical assault, abusive language, intimidation and delays in obtaining medical examination.

At the heart of this controversy are allegations by women journalists against ACP Vivek Bhagat. These are allegations that must be investigated impartially, through the available CCTV footage, videos and other evidence — not buried, delayed or dismissed.

The wider question is even more serious:

If citizens cannot peacefully demand an FIR against a police officer, who protects citizens from the misuse of police power?

And if protesters are allegedly beaten while asking for accountability, the answer cannot be another detention, another warning or another delay.

Delhi Police has said that complaints were received and that the matter was sent to the Crime Branch for investigation, while reports also say CCTV footage is being examined.

That investigation must be independent, transparent and time-bound.

No police officer should receive immunity from accountability merely because the allegation concerns a member of the police force.

No journalist should have to risk physical intimidation simply for recording a detention.

No woman should have to spend hours outside a police station pleading for her complaint to be registered.

And no young citizen should be made to believe that demanding constitutional rights is itself a crime.

The Gen Z generation is watching.

The country is watching.

The answer to peaceful resistance cannot be violence.
The answer to a complaint cannot be intimidation.
The answer to evidence cannot be silence.

Let every available video, CCTV recording, medical report and eyewitness account be preserved.

Let every allegation be investigated fairly.

Let responsibility be fixed wherever wrongdoing is established.

And let the resistance remain peaceful, constitutional and fearless.

WE DO NOT ASK FOR PRIVILEGE.
WE ASK FOR EQUALITY BEFORE THE LAW.
WE ASK FOR ACCOUNTABILITY.
WE ASK FOR JUSTICE.

text:
Beyond Connectivity

As technology reshapes how people live, work, and transact, connectivity is evolving into a broader digital ecosystem. Dialog Axiata has moved beyond its traditional role as a telecommunications provider to build platforms spanning connectivity, digital services, fintech, and AI.

Speaking with Business Today, Group Chief Marketing Officer, Lasantha Theverapperuma discusses how technology can create greater customer value, and the role of people and culture in sustaining transformation. He also looks ahead to the opportunities for digital payments, AI, and connected platforms to accelerate Sri Lanka’s digital economy.

Words: Jennifer Paldano Goonewardane.

Photography: Rasanga Dissanayake.

Dialog has evolved from a telecommunications provider to a quad-play business, a digital enabler, and, increasingly, a fintech player. What has driven this evolution, and how has it changed the role Dialog plays in the everyday lives of its customers?

Over the last 20 to 25 years, customer needs have evolved significantly. Initially, mobile phones were primarily used for making calls. Dialog entered the market at that point and has since looked at how customers and the world were evolving, ensuring that Sri Lankans remained connected to global trends.

We started with broadband, then moved into television, and eventually began integrating these services into an ecosystem. We had mobile, broadband, and TV operating as separate services, and we saw the need to bring them together. As customers became more engaged with this ecosystem, it marked the beginning of our digital journey.

At the same time, we identified fintech opportunities based on customer needs. Customers cannot always go to a bank or retailer to complete every transaction they need. This led us to develop services that addressed those needs.

This evolution has taken place alongside changes in customer behavior and the wider world, with Dialog playing a role in that journey. Our purpose is to empower and enrich all Sri Lankans, advancing people and the country. That purpose has guided the steps we have taken over the past 25 years.

Digital ecosystems are ultimately about making customers’ lives simpler and more connected. How is Dialog bringing together its different digital capabilities to create a more seamless experience across the customer journey?

Ultimately, it is about customer satisfaction, regardless of our digital capabilities. There are two main areas we focus on. One is the product itself. We have to ensure that we provide a product that meets the customer’s needs.

Alongside the product, we have to make sure customers can access it, raise concerns, resolve issues, and receive service with as little effort as possible. We look at how we can reduce the customer’s transactional costs, including the time and hassle of going through lengthy processes to resolve an issue.

When these two come together – a good product and easy access to service – customers should be able to resolve an issue, access a service, purchase a product, or clarify a bill or product-related matter within seconds.

Bringing the product and service experience together in this way improves customer satisfaction and builds trust. Customers need to know that the product works and that any concerns or questions can be resolved quickly. This trust is what we are focused on building across the ecosystem, which ultimately leads to Brand Love, an important outcome for us.

From a CMO perspective, our focus is on ensuring that we address every part of the customer journey and deliver a seamless experience.

You mentioned building “Brand Love” as an important outcome. Where does Dialog stand in that journey today, and what are you doing to strengthen that connection with customers?

It is a journey. All of us are working towards it, and we are doing several things across the business to get there.

Take the launch of 5G, for example. We are behind some of our peers in Asia, but once the licenses were issued, we deployed more than 1,000 sites within six months, allowing customers to experience the technology. That is one example from the product side.

Today, we cover 99 percent of the population, but 5G does not yet reach everyone. There are customers who are still not covered, and that is part of the journey we have embarked on through continued investment and finding the right balance to achieve wider coverage.

We are investing to ensure customer satisfaction. At the same time, across our digital apps and customer journeys, we are working to improve the experience as much as possible.

Every portfolio at Dialog is on a journey towards building Brand Love.

AI is rapidly reshaping the way businesses engage with customers. Beyond automation and efficiency, where do you see AI creating the greatest value in making customer experience simpler, more intuitive, and more relevant?

AI is a buzzword today, but we look at it more broadly. For us, the question is what value AI can create, and ultimately, that means value for the customer.

AI can bring efficiencies to the business, but in Sri Lanka, where we have access to labor, the opportunity is not necessarily about reducing costs. It is more about improving efficiency. On the customer side, however, there is much greater potential, particularly in reducing the transactional cost and making information more accessible.

For example, when you call a contact center today, you go through several steps before reaching an agent – selecting a language, verifying your number, and providing additional information. By the time you explain the problem, the process itself can create frustration.

We have addressed part of this through the MyDialog app, which allows customers to manage their mobile, television, and broadband services, monitor usage, make payments, and reload their accounts. The next step is our AI-enabled chatbot, DIA, available through WhatsApp. A customer can simply ask to check their balance in Sinhala, Tamil, or English, select the relevant account, and receive the information within seconds. Because the interaction starts on the customer’s phone, there is no need to repeat the verification process.

We are also applying AI in other areas. Govi Mithuru, for example, enables farmers to scan a plant, identify potential diseases, and receive advice on what action to take. Customers can also ask questions by voice. The objective is to make information easier to access and more relevant to their needs.

Our approach to AI is also about bridging AI platforms with local information. Platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini do not necessarily have access to this information. Our role as a technology enabler is to bridge that gap.

For example, Sri Lankan agriculture has its own conditions, including differences in soil and cultivation practices. Govi Mithuru brings together relevant information from the agriculture sector and AI to provide guidance tailored to Sri Lankan farmers. That is where we see an important role for Dialog in applying AI.

As digital payments become part of everyday life, how do you see the convergence of connectivity and financial services reshaping the customer experience and accelerating Sri Lanka’s transition towards a more digital economy?

Dialog’s journey into fintech began in 2012, when we invested in mobile money. The platform enabled retailers and the wider community to make transfers through a digital wallet, which has since evolved.

We later acquired Dialog Finance, adding financing capabilities to the ecosystem. In parallel, our digital ecosystem continued to grow, particularly through the MyDialog app, which now has more than four million monthly active users. We saw an opportunity to bring these capabilities together and make fintech services more accessible to customers.

That is where Dialog Pay comes in. Integrated within the MyDialog app, Dialog Pay brings payments and financial services closer to a platform customers already use in their everyday lives. Customers can make QR payments using funds from any bank account, eZ Cash or a Dialog Finance savings account, across a growing network of more than 100,000 merchant outlets. The focus is on making digital payments simple, accessible and relevant enough to become part of daily transactions. Just as the growth of telecommunications creates value for the wider community, we believe a strong digital economy is essential for Sri Lanka to move to the next level. The Government and banks have important roles to play, but as a telecommunications company with a broad network of customers and retailers, we also play a role in enabling digital transactions.

We have an ecosystem that brings together our digital platforms, retailers, and partners, allowing customers to transact through these channels. Our aim is to take fintech to the next level and contribute to the development of Sri Lanka’s digital economy. That is the direction of our journey and our mission.

Digital transformation extends beyond the end customer to the businesses and retailers that serve them. How is Dialog using its digital capabilities to empower its wider retail and partner ecosystem?

Customers do not evolve in isolation; they are part of a wider ecosystem. In Sri Lanka, the local retailer continues to play an important role. Customers often rely on the storekeeper for advice, information about new products, and guidance on what is available in the market. We recognized this and began looking at how we could digitally empower our retail network.

Five years ago, when a customer wanted to obtain a SIM or connection, the process involved filling out forms, signing documents, and physically sending them for processing. Information then had to be entered manually, which created delays and errors.

Today, that process has been digitized through our Retail Hub app. Retailers can complete connections using the customer’s NIC and photograph, significantly simplifying the process.

We then brought mobile money into the platform, allowing retailers to collect bills, including electricity and water bills.

We subsequently added other services such as government payments and doctor channeling. Today, through Dialog Pay, retailers can also accept payments and make transfers via QR code.

Retailers are an important part of our ecosystem. We have around 100,000 retailers across the country, and we are continuing to bring the digital capabilities we develop, including AI, into that network. This creates another path to the customer. We can serve customers directly through our digital platforms, while retailers can also take these services to customers. In that way, the retailer becomes an extension of the digital ecosystem, bringing these services closer to the customer.

With a retail network of this scale and turnover, how does Dialog maintain consistent standards, governance, and security across its retailers?

We have a governance unit that oversees the retailer ecosystem, which is important given its scale. We have around 100,000 retailers, with approximately 2,500 new retailers joining and a similar number leaving each month as businesses cease operations or change.

We also have a distributor network of nearly 1,000 people who regularly visit retailers. They ensure that retailers follow our processes, replenish stocks, and address any gaps in knowledge or training.

With a network of this size, we cannot simply issue instructions from the center and expect them to be followed. Our distributor network serves as the link between Dialog and retailers, ensuring they maintain the required standards and are equipped to serve customers effectively.

Building a digital ecosystem requires marketing, technology, data, product, operations, and customer experience to work increasingly as a single, cohesive ecosystem. How does this change the way established organizations need to operate and lead?

There are two aspects to this. First, building a digital ecosystem requires specialized skills. We have dedicated teams for areas such as AI and analytics, technology, and other specialized functions, each led by a leader. This allows these teams to move quickly within their respective areas of expertise.

At the same time, we have recognized the need for a horizontal layer that brings these specialized functions together. The end result is not the work of one division; it is about combining these capabilities to create customer value. That requires leaders who can connect the different areas and understand how they work together.

These leaders need experience in their respective disciplines, but they also need cross-functional knowledge. An AI or analytics specialist, for example, needs to understand the business requirement, the customer perspective, and how technology can be applied to address it. Marketing, customer service, technology, engineering, and business need to come together.

That is why we encourage our leaders to move across different parts of the organization and gain practical experience. This cannot be learned from a textbook alone. You need to work within these functions and understand their objectives and challenges.

In my case, I started in finance, then moved into strategy, business leadership, operations, and digital, and now into marketing. That experience has helped me understand how different functions look at the same issue.

For example, when finance raises concerns about spending, I understand the perspective behind that. Similarly, when evaluating a customer proposition, I consider what we can invest, the value we are creating, and the return on that investment. There needs to be a balance between what we want to deliver and what the business can sustain.

Digital ecosystems require the same balance. We serve customers directly, through retailers, and through partners, so we need to understand the customer and the role of each part of the ecosystem.

Increasingly, I believe organizations need a layer of leadership that connects the customer to the organization’s different functions. That ability to connect these areas is an important differentiator.

With such a diverse customer base and a growing number of products, how are data and AI changing the way Dialog segments customers and measures the effectiveness of its marketing?

I think it is promising rather than challenging. If you go back ten years, marketing was largely one-way communication. An advertisement would be developed, approved internally, and placed on television or radio. We would then use surveys to understand the response, but there was limited visibility into how customers were actually responding.

Today, as soon as we run an advertisement or marketing communication, we can see whether it is working and gather customer feedback. That allows us to make decisions and adjust our approach much faster.

It also allows us to target different customer groups. For example, if we are marketing a product such as Air Fiber, we know the target group and can direct the communication to those customers rather than communicating to the entire market. Analytics and AI allow us to segment customers and use those profiles to deliver the right communication to the right audience.

The communication itself can also be tailored, whether in Sinhala, Tamil, or English, so that customers receive information relevant to them. We can identify which channels to invest in, determine how much to invest, and measure the return from each channel.

The marketing budget itself may not necessarily come down. The reason is that the number of products and propositions we offer has increased significantly. Today, we have hundreds of products, so we need to understand which products are relevant to which customers.

The objective is therefore not necessarily to spend less, but to make the investment more effective. Instead of offering one product to everyone, we can identify what is relevant to each customer and communicate accordingly.

Technology can be acquired, but transformation ultimately depends on people. What kind of culture and mindset will organizations need to continually evolve as technology and customer expectations change?

Technology today is largely accessible to everyone. Our competitors and we can have similar technology stacks. The differentiator is the people who use that technology and how they create value for customers.

Technology is an enabler; it will not create that value on its own. To make the most of it, organizations need a culture that enables people to work towards a common purpose.

Culture will continue to evolve, but the fundamentals should remain consistent. There needs to be a clear purpose for the organization’s existence and how each employee contributes to it. When people understand the organization’s purpose and where it is going, they can work towards a common goal.

At Dialog, we focus on empowering our people, particularly the younger generation. The world is changing quickly, and someone who joins the organization today may have knowledge that is more relevant to a particular issue than someone who has been there for years. We therefore want everyone to have an equal opportunity to contribute ideas and challenge existing thinking.

Hierarchical organizations can limit this. At Dialog, we try to reduce those barriers. The CEO, CXOs, and other employees work together, and we are willing to listen to someone who has recently joined the organization because that person may have knowledge that can contribute to a decision.

That requires respect, equal opportunity, and a willingness to learn from one another. Beyond the common purpose that holds the organization together, the culture needs to remain fluid enough to allow people to contribute and bring out their best.

Employee mobility is also part of organizational continuity. How does Dialog balance the movement of people with the need to retain knowledge, culture, and a sense of purpose within the organization?

I see people moving between organizations or jobs as part of a natural cycle. Younger employees may leave to gain more exposure, experience, or benefits, and I encourage that. If you look at my own career, I have rarely stayed in the same role for more than two or three years. I have been at Dialog for 22 years, but I have moved across different roles and functions.

I moved because I wanted to see what was beyond what I was already doing. That helps an individual evolve, expand their knowledge, and develop professionally. Moving between organizations can be part of that same journey.

One reason I stayed at Dialog is that I could see opportunities to move across functions. I joined finance, my core area, then moved into strategy, digital transformation, operations and eventually into my current role as Group Chief Marketing Officer. We try to create similar opportunities for people within Dialog through cross-functional movements. As a large organization, we can move people across divisions. We also have programs where employees can apply to move to another division at a higher level.

So, if people want to move, we try to create opportunities for them to do so within the organization. At the same time, even when people leave, if we maintain a clear purpose and mission, they take that with them. They have contributed to the organization, learned from it, and, in turn, helped develop it.

I don’t see people who leave after two or three years as a loss. They have contributed while they were here, and someone else comes in to continue the journey. Some will stay and eventually take on greater leadership roles. The people who move in and out also contribute to the organization’s evolution.

It is therefore important that we respect that movement. If we question why someone has stayed only two or three years, that creates the wrong attitude. People should be given the opportunity to grow, whether that growth happens within the organization or elsewhere.

Looking ahead, how do you see the convergence of connectivity, digital platforms, payments, and AI shaping the next phase of Sri Lanka’s digital economy? And what role can companies such as Dialog Pay in enabling that future?

Sri Lanka is an island, and in some ways, we can be complacent because we are comfortable with what we have. That can slow the adoption of new technologies and transformations.

For example, people may be used to going to a shop and transacting with cash. We have 5G today, but many people will continue using their existing phones because they are comfortable with them. That is part of our culture. But in an increasingly digital world, we also need to accelerate our adoption of technology and new trends.

Bridging that divide is part of Dialog’s role. The Government is introducing many reforms, and with access to around 20 million customers, 100,000 retailers, and a thousand people in the field, we believe we have a responsibility to help bridge that gap.

It is not about changing our culture, but about retaining what is valuable while moving towards a more digital economy. That requires a balance between the two. Digital ecosystems, AI, and digital platforms can help bridge that gap.

Our digital tools, such as Govi Mithuru, DIA, the MyDialog app, and Retail Hub, can help Sri Lankans become more comfortable with digital services. This is also why we have entered the fintech space. Through Dialog Pay, we are bringing together our digital and financial services capabilities to make digital payments simpler and more accessible for customers, while helping drive greater adoption of cashless transactions.

Digital payments, particularly QR payments, are still in their early stages in Sri Lanka. There is a significant gap compared with markets such as India and China. As digital payments and fintech adoption increase, there can also be economic benefits from greater efficiency and reduced costs associated with handling and transporting cash.

This evolution has already started and is accelerating. Dialog plays an important role in that journey. Our mission is to empower and enrich Sri Lankan lives and enterprises, and we need to be part of taking the country towards the next stage of its digital economy.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo
